title: Last Seen Now Knows When You Were On MFL
summary: The Owner Activity page used to know one thing about you: whether you had loaded a page on this site. It now also knows when you last logged into MFL — an actual timestamp, straight from MFL — and ranks everybody by whichever happened more recently. Owners who live inside MFL and rarely come here stop showing up as ghosts.
description: There has always been a hole in Owner Activity. It measured exactly one thing — whether you had opened a page on this site — and then cheerfully labeled anyone who hadn't as Dormant. Which was fine, except that half this league does its business inside MFL and only wanders over here to look at rosters or check the standings once a month. Those owners were logging in, setting lineups and working the wire, and getting a red dot for it.

So Last Seen now watches both. MFL keeps its own last-login timestamp for every franchise, and the page reads it: your row is ranked by whichever came later, your last visit here or your last time on MFL. Each row shows its work — the blended time up top with a small badge saying which one won, then both raw numbers underneath, plus what your most recent roster move was and when. An owner sitting at "Site: never" and "MFL: 4h ago" is exactly the person this was built to stop mislabeling.

There is a nice bit of trivia buried in this one. That last-login number is not in MFL's documentation. It is not in any of their fifty-nine published data feeds, and it is not in the franchise record everybody else can see — we checked sixty other leagues to be sure. It turns up only when the request comes from a commissioner, which is how it sat there unnoticed for years. It syncs over every six hours now.

For the leagues and moments where that number isn't available, the page falls back to your last roster move — a trade, a free agent pickup, a waiver claim, an auction bid, an IR or taxi shuffle. Two things it deliberately never counts: moves the commissioner made on your behalf, because the commish fixing your lineup is not evidence you were awake, and the league-wide automatic stuff like the kickoff lock and the scheduled waiver run, which fires for every team in the league every week and would have made everybody look permanently active.
imageAlt: The Owner Activity page's Last Seen table. Each row gives a team, a blended last-seen time with a small badge reading SITE or MFL, and a smaller line underneath breaking out all three signals — for example Cowboy Up, ranked seventh at "4 hours ago" with an MFL badge, over "Site: never · MFL: 4h ago · Last move: 9h ago (taxi squad move)". A green Active status dot sits at the right of each row.

title: Ten Quiet Minutes And The Big Board Starts Talking To Itself
summary: An email draft can leave one crest on the TV for six hours. Now, after ten minutes with nothing picked, the board runs a highlight cycle — the roster of whoever is on the clock, then the team on deck, then every position that is off the board, then the whole draft replayed from 1.01. The second somebody actually picks, it drops everything and cuts to the live reveal.
description: The Draft Broadcast was built for a room: a pick lands, the player takes the whole screen over his franchise's colors, everybody looks up. That works beautifully on a night where the picks are ninety seconds apart. It works considerably less beautifully on an email draft, where the rules allow eight hours per selection and the television spends the entire evening showing one crest, one name, and an ELAPSED clock climbing past 2:41:19 like a hostage video.

So the board now entertains itself. Ten minutes with nothing picked and it starts a cycle, and it leads with the two things the room is actually arguing about while it waits. What has the man on the clock already got? — his whole roster, keepers and tonight's picks together, laid out by position with the faces, so the four running backs and the empty tight end row are visible from the back of the room. Then the same for whoever is on deck, because the next argument starts before the current one ends.

Then what is off the board: every position taken tonight, counted, ranked and drawn with the faces of the men who went there. That is the fact nobody can reconstruct in a draft that runs over days — the run on running backs happened on Tuesday and the only record of it is a group chat nobody is going to scroll on a television.

And then the rewind: the draft replayed from 1.01, every selection in order, eight seconds each, the same full-screen reveal it got when it was news. A chip in the corner reads REWIND · PICK 12 OF 47 so nobody mistakes history for a pick that just landed, and it carries who is actually on the clock the whole way through.

When the cycle runs out, the on-the-clock board comes back. Ten more quiet minutes and it goes again. And the instant a real selection lands on MFL, all of it is over mid-card — the live reveal wins, always, which is the only rule this thing has. A draft that is actually moving will never see it at all. It runs on both boards with nothing to turn on; if you want the old behavior for a night, ?screensaver=off pins the board to the on-the-clock screen and nothing else.
imageAlt: The Draft Broadcast in full screen showing a franchise roster panel, painted in the Boondock Saints' deep red. The header reads ON DECK over a large “Boondock Saints”, with the franchise crest to its left and “7 on the roster” underneath. Three rows follow, each a position label and a count beside a line of player headshots in team-colored circles: QB 1 (Daniels), RB 4 (Achane, Henry, Skattebo, Walker III) and WR 2 (Brown, Egbuka).

title: The Room Can Now See Exactly How Long You've Been Thinking
summary: The big board told the room who was on the clock and said it in precisely the same way at eight seconds and at eight minutes. It now counts up from the last pick, so everybody watching the TV knows exactly how long a man has been sitting there.
description: Between picks, the Draft Broadcast has always answered one question very well and refused to answer the other one at all. Whose turn it is: crest the size of a dinner plate, name above it, ON THE CLOCK underneath, unmissable from the far end of the room. How long it has been his turn: nothing. The screen looked identical eight seconds after a pick and eight minutes after it, which meant the only instrument the room had was somebody eventually saying “is he even here?”

So the board now runs a clock. Under the pick number there is an ELAPSED chip counting up from the moment the previous selection landed — 0:09, 4:12, and if a round genuinely goes that way, 1:05:07. It snaps back to 0:00 the instant the next team comes up, so the number on screen is always this team's, never the last one's.

It counts from MFL's own timestamp on the previous pick, not from whenever this page happened to open, and that distinction is the whole feature. Somebody's laptop dying and getting reloaded in round four does not hand the man on the clock a fresh three minutes — the board comes back up already knowing he has been thinking for six. Before the first pick of the night it stays away entirely, because “First on the clock” has nothing to count from, and once the last pick is in it leaves with the rest of the furniture.

Nothing else about draft night changes. Keep making your picks in MFL, keep the board plugged into the TV, and keep the predictor open on a second screen if you like being told what is about to happen to you. The clock is simply the room's answer to a question it was already asking out loud.
imageAlt: The Draft Broadcast board for The League in full screen, painted in the Pacific Pigskins' deep red. The Pigskins' boar crest fills the left half of the stage, and to its right the copy reads “Pacific Pigskins” in small type over a large “On the clock”, then “Pick 1.10”, and beneath that a dark rounded chip labelled ELAPSED showing 0:08 in fixed-width digits. The header runs “THE LEAGUE” on the left and “PICK 10 OF 51 · 3 ROUNDS × 17” on the right. Along the bottom, JUST OFF THE BOARD lists 1.09 KC Concepcion (WR · CLE), 1.08 Eli Stowers (TE · PHI), 1.07 Fernando Mendoza (QB · LV) and 1.06 Makai Lemon (WR · PHI), each with the player's headshot and the drafting franchise's crest, while UP NEXT lists 1.11 Dark Magicians, 1.12 Vitside and 1.13 Da Dangsters.

title: Rookie Draft Night Gets A Television
summary: Plug a laptop into the TV and let the room watch the rookie draft happen. Keep making your picks in MFL exactly like always — this board just watches the same draft you are in, and puts every selection on screen seconds later: the player, the crest of the team that took him, and how far down the board he was when somebody reached.
description: Three rounds, fifty-one picks, and for years the only way to know what went was to watch somebody's face change. The picks live inside MFL on sixteen separate laptops, which is fine for drafting and useless for a room. So here is the Draft Broadcast — a page with exactly one job, which is to be plugged into a television and looked at.

Nothing about how you draft changes. Keep making picks in MFL. This board just watches the same draft you are in: a few seconds after a selection lands, the player takes over the whole screen in his new franchise's colors, crest behind him, position and college and bye week underneath. Between picks it tells the room who is on the clock and who is up next, and it keeps the screen awake so the TV does not go dark in the middle of round two.

The line that will start arguments is board rank — where the guy sat in the rookie class when his name got called. Taken well ahead of it and the screen says so. Still the top name available and it says Best Available, which is the polite way of announcing that everyone else left him there. It is ranked against the rookie class specifically, not against every free agent in the league, so 1.01 reads like 1.01 instead of like the 300th-best asset on the board.

It is live during the draft, and there is a rehearse mode that replays last year's draft pick by pick — worth running once before the night, if only to see the 1.01 land again. Once the picks are in, the draft room still holds the full board and the draft order still holds next year's.
imageAlt: The Draft Broadcast page for The League, filling a widescreen display. A pick reveal is on screen: the eyebrow line reads “WITH THE 1.01, COWBOY UP SELECT” above the player name “Ashton Jeanty” in large condensed type, then a row giving his position RB, his college Boise State, and BYE 8. A green “BEST AVAILABLE” badge sits below, and under it “BOARD RANK” over a large “#1”. The drafting franchise’s crest is watermarked large behind the text over a deep red-to-navy gradient in that franchise’s colors, with a faint “1.01” numeral across the lower left.

title: Your Board, On The Actual Draft Board
summary: The rankings board now talks to MFL. Build your order here, hit push, and it becomes the My Draft List your draft room reads off — the same list that sits there at 3am when the clock is running and you are not awake to defend yourself.
description: There has always been a gap between the board you build and the board that drafts for you. You would spend an evening sorting players on My Draft List, then open MFL and hand-type the whole thing into a different list, in a different order, on a different screen. Most people did it once and then never again, which is how a carefully built board turns into an autopick taking the best available kicker.

That gap is closed. The board pulls your existing draft list down from MFL, and pushes your order back up to it — the real one, the one the Live Draft Room reads. Your previous list is saved before anything is overwritten, so an undo is one tap away, and the confirmation tells you exactly how many players are about to be written before you commit to anything. Seed it from the sources you already picked on Import Rankings, drag it into the shape you want, push it, go to bed.

There is also a filter for the players you can actually draft, which is a shorter list than you think. In a rookie-draft league it is the rookies; in a league that drafts everyone it is anyone not already sitting on a roster in your conference — and it knows the difference, so a player another conference owns is still yours to take. Turn the filter on and it limits the push too: what you see is what gets written. No more discovering on draft night that a third of your board is on somebody else's roster.
imageAlt: The My Draft List board with Pull from MFL and Push to MFL controls above a ranked player list

title: Put The Draft On The Big Screen
summary: Plug a laptop into the TV and let the room watch the draft happen. Every pick made in MFL lands on screen seconds later — the player, his new team's colors and crest, and exactly how far down the board he was when somebody grabbed him.
description: Draft night has always had the same problem: the picks happen inside MFL, on twelve separate laptops, and the room has no idea what just went until somebody says it out loud. So here is the Draft Broadcast — a page with one job, which is to be plugged into a TV and looked at.

Keep making your picks in MFL exactly like always. Nothing about that changes. This board just watches the same draft you're in and reacts to it: a few seconds after a selection lands, the player takes over the whole screen in the colors of the team that just took him, with his crest behind him. Position, pro team, bye week, what he's projected for. Take a team defense and the screen doesn't go empty where a man should be — two of that unit's actual stars turn up shoulder to shoulder, the same marquee defenders the free agent board puts in front of you, and they get the pick. A helmet is not a face, and nobody should have to guess who Denver's pass rush is.

And the line the room is going to argue about: where he actually stood when his name got called. BEST AVAILABLE means nobody left on the board was rated higher — that one turns green. 14th best available means thirteen better men were sitting right there. The board doesn't call it a steal and it doesn't call it a reach; it tells you the number and lets twelve people draw their own conclusions, loudly. The one thing it will not do is measure you against a draft you aren't in — with seven keepers per team the good players are gone before 1.01 is even called, so this counts only the men who were genuinely available to you.

Between picks the board keeps the room oriented — who's on the clock, what just came off, who's warming up next, in the order the draft order set months ago. Because the AFL drafts by conference, there's a board for each: open the American League or the National League, whichever one is actually running that night, and flip between them at the bottom. Hit Full Screen and the site disappears entirely.
Built for Saturday. Everything on it comes off the same MFL draft you're already in, so there is nothing to set up — open it and it follows along.
imageAlt: The AFL Draft Broadcast board on a TV, showing which franchise is on the clock over its team colors and crest, with the last four picks and the next three teams up.

title: The #1 Seed Is A Trap
summary: Nineteen seasons of evidence that the best regular season buys you almost nothing. The #1 seed has won the title 4 times out of 19. Pulling a champion's name out of a hat hits about 6%. That's the entire edge for a first-round bye and home-field-that-isn't: fifteen points of probability, and a lot of teams who found out the hard way.
description: Every year somebody clinches the top seed in November and starts talking like the trophy is in the mail. Playoff Performance is the page that shuts that down. Every completed season from 2007 to 2025, the #1 seed next to the team that actually won it, and a running tally of how rarely those are the same name.

Four for nineteen. Twenty-one percent. And it is worse than the number looks, because three of those four came in a row — 2022, 2023, 2024 — which means that across the first fifteen years of this league the top seed won exactly once. Then 2025 arrived and the 15-3 Wabbits handed the thing to the Computer Jocks, who were nobody's idea of a favorite.

The best exhibit is still 2018. The Wascawy Wabbits went 16-0. Sixteen and zero. They did not win the championship. They did not reach the final. Under Siege did, and Under Siege had spent the regular season at 8-8 — go pull it up on the playoff bracket if you don't believe it.

The secondary view asks whether all-play — every team measured against every other team's score, week by week, which strips out whether your schedule was kind — knows something the standings don't. Barely. The all-play leader has won 5 of 19, and across 9 of the 19 seasons the all-play leader and the top seed were the same team anyway. Being demonstrably the best is worth about five extra points of title odds over being lucky, which is not the answer anybody wants.

One note on how the #1 seed is decided here, because it matters and it bit us: we read it off the bracket — whoever took the first-round bye — not off the standings page. Those disagree. In 2008 and 2010 the team sitting in row one of the standings was not the team that got the bye. The games know who was seeded first; the table doesn't always.
imageAlt: The Playoff Performance page for The League in dark mode, headed “Does the best regular season win anything?” over the line “19 completed seasons, 2007–2025. The #1 seed has won the title 4 of 19 times. Picking a champion at random out of a hat would hit about 6% of the time.” Below sit four cards: “#1 seed wins the title” showing 21%, 4 of 19, with a note that it reached the final 7 of 19; “All-play leader wins the title” showing 26%, 5 of 19, reaching the final 9 of 19; “Same team held both” showing 9 of 19, the #1 seed also being the all-play leader; and “Random baseline” showing 6%, one team in 16. A “Season by season” table follows, noting all-play is cut at the end of the regular season — week 14 in recent years, week 13 before 2021 — with columns for Year, #1 seed, All-play leader, Champion and Result. The 2025 row lists the Wascawy Wabbits at 15-3 as top seed, Da Dangsters leading all-play at .729, Computer Jocks as champion, and a grey “neither” tag. The 2024, 2023 and 2022 rows each show one team sweeping all three columns — Wascawy Wabbits at 14-4 and .714, Fire Ready Aim at 15-3 and .762, and Vitside Mafia at 15-3 and .762 — every one of them carrying both a blue “#1 seed” tag and an “all-play” tag.
